overview: Adal was a Muslim political formation in the Horn of Africa associated with centers including Dakar and Harar. Its changing political geography must be separated from the histories of individual cities and continuing communities.

items.text: Harar’s street pattern follows a sixteenth-century design, with commercial and religious buildings around its center and a network of narrow lanes.
Harar’s defensive walls developed between the thirteenth and sixteenth centuries. They are an urban monument, not a surviving map of Adal’s entire territory.
The older Library of Congress account describes Saylac as a center of schools, mosques and regional trade. Its institutional history extended beyond Adal’s changing capitals.
Harari weaving, basketry and bookbinding remain living traditions. UNESCO does not date every surviving technique or townhouse to Adal’s rule.
Treccani describes a sixteenth-century shift toward Aussa and subsequent division into Aussa and Harar polities. This transition is broader than the death of one military leader.
